newsitem.title: USA: New study shows a drop in television violence.
newsitem.headline: New study shows a drop in television violence.

text.p: Major U.S. television networks aired less violence in the latest season after several offending series were either cancelled or cleaned up, according to a study released on Tuesday.

But the study, by the UCLA Centre for Communication Policy, also cited continued high levels of violence in made-for-TV movies and theatrical films on TV. It singled out the independent channel UPN for airing almost as many offending series as all the other networks combined.

The UPN channel, jointly owned by Viacom Inc and Chris-Craft Industries Inc, broadcast four series deemed to raise frequent concerns about violence, it said. That compared with five offending series from the 181 hours of weekly programming produced by the four major television networks.
UPN, by comparison, runs only six hours of original programming per week.
The University of California at Los Angeles study also attacked UPN for actively promoting its violence, with the tag "Lethal Wednesday" for its bloodiest night of programming.

The study, funded by ABC, NBC, CBS and Fox, monitored every network prime time and Saturday morning entertainment programme aired in the 1995-96 television season. It also surveyed local and syndicated television, public television, basic and pay cable, home video, video games played on television and the new UPN and WB independent channels.
"Violence on television is still a serious problem," said Jeff Cole, director of the UCLA Centre for Communication Policy. "But in no way has network television gotten worse."

Cole said he believed the government played a role in the improvement and cited two summits on the matter hosted by President Bill Clinton as well as speeches by Republican presidential contender Bob Dole.
